seasons.title: What you notice
seasons.question: What decides what we actually see and hear?
seasons.assumption: That perceiving is passive and complete: that what is in front of a person simply arrives.
seasons.contrasts: A drum maker listening for a tone against a coir worker whose product nobody looks at; a puppeteer's hand that the audience never watches against a bird counter who must take a flock one at a time.
seasons.shift: Attention is an act with a cost, and it selects. By the end of the season the audience has watched several people whose whole skill is a way of attending, and one place where the attending is itself doing damage.
seasons.prepares: If seeing is selective, the next question is what the selection turns things into.
seasons.ep1_effect: Episode 1 was watched before any of this. On a second viewing the monastery sequence reads as somebody learning to attend, not somebody arriving somewhere.

seasons.title: What you take a thing to be
seasons.question: When does recognising something become deciding what it is?
seasons.assumption: That a confident recognition is the same as understanding.
seasons.contrasts: A tune that sells bread without anyone looking at the bread, against a disease recognised by its signs for thirty years with no agreed cause; a guide who sees what a visitor cannot, against a law that turned a way of living into an offence.
seasons.shift: Recognition can be fast, firm, useful and still carry no understanding, and the names it produces can outlast the thing they described.
seasons.prepares: If a name can stick to a person, so can a want. The next season turns to what people reach for.
seasons.ep1_effect: The monastery in Episode 1 is a place the audience recognised instantly. This season makes that instant recognition suspect.

seasons.title: Wanting, having and enough
seasons.question: What keeps something wanted after the cost of it is clear?
seasons.assumption: That wanting is simple, and that people who keep wanting something have not understood what it costs.
seasons.contrasts: Pilgrims who walk for two months carrying almost nothing, against a safari driver whose income depends on producing a leopard; a tea taster whose palate is a calibration, against a freelancer whose income separates them from their street.
seasons.shift: Wanting is not one thing. It can be a reason to go without, a trap built by an incentive, or a measurement against whatever you happen to be used to.
seasons.prepares: Wanting something does not produce the effort to get it. The next season is about what does.
seasons.ep1_effect: Whatever Chathura went to the monastery for, this season makes it harder to call it renunciation.

seasons.title: Effort, readiness and the conditions for acting
seasons.question: What has to be true before a person can act at all?
seasons.assumption: That effort is a matter of will, and that people who do not act have not decided to.
seasons.contrasts: A tapper climbing before the heat against a salt worker who cannot hurry the sun; an ambulance crew whose skill is measured in seconds against a household that has been told its house is unsafe and has not moved.
seasons.shift: Readiness is made of conditions: a body, a season, a price, a road, a rule. Deciding is not moving.
seasons.prepares: If acting depends on conditions, so does learning. The next season asks how anyone can tell they are getting better.
seasons.ep1_effect: Arriving at a monastery is an act with conditions behind it, and Episode 100 will show what they were.

seasons.title: Learning, mastery and the judgement of progress
seasons.question: How do we know whether we are getting anywhere?
seasons.assumption: That progress can be measured, and that someone qualified can tell you where you are.
seasons.contrasts: A dancer whose teacher decides when he may wear the costume, against a lighthouse keeper with nobody to judge him; a ten-year-old sitting a national examination, against a weaving village counting how many households are left.
seasons.shift: Some learning cannot be described, some cannot be examined, and some of what looks like arrival is a place you passed through.
seasons.prepares: Having a skill raises the question of what it is for, and who it is given to.
seasons.ep1_effect: Nothing in Episode 1 tells the audience whether Chathura is a beginner. This season makes that a real question rather than an assumption.

seasons.title: Giving and what moves it
seasons.question: What is actually happening when somebody gives something away?
seasons.assumption: That generosity is self-explanatory, and that the act tells you the reason.
seasons.contrasts: A dansal that gives away everything it makes, against a stall on a mountain trail that is both devotion and a business; a blood donor who gives what they need, against men paid to guard the eggs they used to sell.
seasons.shift: The same act carries different reasons, and some restraint is indistinguishable from generosity until you ask who is watching.
seasons.prepares: Restraint when nobody is watching leads directly to fairness when everybody is.
seasons.ep1_effect: A monastery runs on other people's giving. Episode 1 never shows who fed anyone.

seasons.title: Conscience, fairness and what is shared
seasons.question: How does something held in common become something that can be taken?
seasons.assumption: That unfairness is caused by bad people, and that naming the cause is straightforward.
seasons.contrasts: A river mined at night in breach of a court order, against a village that hands one person the power to open a sluice; a policy decided quickly and paid for over years, against a market where a night's price is taken over from whatever everyone else is doing.
seasons.shift: Division is a process, not a villain. Fear, custom, incentive and a single confident decision all do the work that gets blamed on greed.
seasons.prepares: If fairness is this hard between strangers, the next season asks what it looks like between people who are responsible for each other.
seasons.ep1_effect: Chathura arrives somewhere that is outside all of this, which is a position that has to be paid for by someone.

seasons.title: Care and the limits of helping
seasons.question: When is stepping back a way of caring, and when is it not?
seasons.assumption: That care means closeness, and that more of it is always better.
seasons.contrasts: Keepers who deliberately minimise contact with the animals they are raising, against a woman who leaves the country so that her family can stay in it; a dog that a street half-owns, against a person who has to travel a hundred kilometres to renew a prescription.
seasons.shift: Care has a shape and a limit. Some of it works by withdrawing, some of it never arrives, and some of it is being done by people nobody is looking at.
seasons.prepares: Every one of these relationships ends. The next season is about what that does.
seasons.ep1_effect: Episode 1 shows a person who has stepped away from everyone. This season makes that neither noble nor cold by default.

seasons.title: Loss, ending and what can still be done
seasons.question: What is left to do for something that has already ended?
seasons.assumption: That grief is a phase that closes, and that an answer or a payment can close it.
seasons.contrasts: A family holding an almsgiving for someone who cannot receive it, against families who refuse a sum of money because they were asking a different question; mangroves replanted where a farm destroyed them, against a village now under a reservoir.
seasons.shift: Repair changes the weight of the past without erasing it, and some of what people do after a loss is not repair at all but a way of continuing to attend.
seasons.prepares: If what is gone does not simply close, the last season can ask what continuity actually is.
seasons.ep1_effect: Episode 1 ends with a disappearance. This season teaches the audience not to read a disappearance as an ending.

seasons.title: Change, memory and returning
seasons.question: What makes something still the same thing after everything in it has been replaced?
seasons.assumption: That a place, a craft or a person is a fixed thing that either survives or does not.
seasons.contrasts: A casting method in which the original must be destroyed to make the object, against a workshop in its fifth generation; a coastline that is wearing away, against a railway that stays the same by being continuously replaced.
seasons.shift: Continuity is made of replacement. What returns to a place does not find the place, and the series ends at the end of a line that was destroyed and rebuilt on its own formation.
seasons.prepares: Nothing. This is where the public journey stops and Episode 100 begins.
seasons.ep1_effect: Everything. By this point the audience has been taught that a return is not a recovery, which is exactly the reading Episode 100 needs them to bring to Episode 1.

SL-SQ01-001.title: The hand the audience does not watch
SL-SQ01-001.premise: UNESCO inscribed Rukada Natya on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2018, the first Sri Lankan element on that list. The inscription records that it is performed by family groups belonging to or connected with the Gamwari lineage in these towns, that puppeteers make their own puppets and handwritten scripts, and that performances have traditionally been held
SL-SQ01-001.activity: Carving and stringing puppets; writing and reciting scripts; a small band; a performance where the audience watches the figure and not the hands above it.
SL-SQ01-001.change: An inscribed tradition with a declining number of practising families; the May-June performance season is a real, datable window.
SL-SQ01-001.unresolved: How many Gamwari families still perform, and whether any performance is scheduled in the coming May-June window. Not established.
SL-SQ01-001.access: No contact made. The UNESCO file names museums as a route, which is a formal and appropriate first approach.
SL-SQ01-001.ethics: An inscribed heritage element attracts attention that can distort it. Filming must not become another demand on a small number of families.

SL-SQ01-002.title: What the rope is made of
SL-SQ01-002.premise: Coir craft is documented in these named Kalutara villages. Sector sources describe coir as a long-established cottage industry, with spinning and weaving employing large numbers regionally, many of them women working part-time, alongside about 10,000 direct and 20,000 indirect jobs in the Sri Lankan coir sector.
SL-SQ01-002.place: Pohaddaramulla, Waskaduwa, Narampitiyawa, Pothupitiya and Panadura
SL-SQ01-002.activity: Retting, beating and cleaning fibre, spinning yarn, twisting rope, drying yards; the difference between hand work and mill work in the same district.
SL-SQ01-002.change: Not established as a current event. The live question is what share of the work is still done by hand and by whom.
SL-SQ01-002.unresolved: Whether hand rope-twisting still happens in these villages or has moved entirely to mills. Not established. Employment figures come from mixed regional sources and must not be attributed to one village.
SL-SQ01-002.ethics: Retting work is wet, low-paid and often women's work. It must not be filmed as texture for a sequence about something else.

SL-SQ01-003.title: The slow way between two towns
SL-SQ01-003.premise: The waterway, known locally as the Dutch canal, runs about 14.5 km in the Negombo section of a longer system reaching Puttalam and Colombo. Dutch works extended an older canal as far as Negombo, recorded by 1706; the British-built Hamilton canal from the Kelani river to Negombo was completed in 1802, named after a revenue agent, and was built partly to drain the Muthurajawela wetland. Flat-bottome
SL-SQ01-003.place: The canal from the Kelani river to Negombo, through the Muthurajawela wetland
SL-SQ01-003.activity: A boat moving at walking pace beside a main road, fishing in the canal, and the wetland it drains.
SL-SQ01-003.change: Not a current event. The material is a 200-year-old piece of infrastructure still in use for something other than what it was built for.
SL-SQ01-003.unresolved: Whether any cargo still moves on the canal, and who lives on its banks. The sources are heritage and tourism accounts and none describes present-day users.
SL-SQ01-003.ethics: Low. Muthurajawela is a protected wetland with its own access rules.

SL-SQ01-005.title: He points, and you see nothing

Published accounts record that every group entering from the two principal entrances must take a local guide, that guides are recruited from neighbouring villages and trained by the Forest Department, and that these are sought-after positions which have made nearby families stakeholders in the reserve. SL-SQ01-005.unresolved: How many guides there are, what they earn, and how the positions are allocated. Not established, and allocation of a scarce licensed job in a small village is exactly where the interesting material would be.

SL-SQ01-006.access: No contact made. The Central Cultural Fund controls all filming and would have to permit any filming of the frescoes, which visitors may not photograph.
SL-SQ01-006.ethics: Low for people, high for the site. A film crew at the fresco gallery is additional footfall and additional time on the staircase, and the project would be doing the thing it is describing.

SL-SQ02-001.title: Two skins, two voices
SL-SQ02-001.premise: Published accounts describe drum-making settlements near Kandy, one with about 33 families and over 200 artisans supplying schools, temples and dancers, and another at Kuragandeniya in Menikhinna with about 15 families. The same accounts report shortages of hides and of suitable wood.
SL-SQ02-001.place: Kuragandeniya, Menikhinna, and the drum-making settlements near Kandy
SL-SQ02-001.activity: Hollowing a single block of jak, kohomba, ehela or red sandalwood; preparing and mounting two different vellums so that the two heads sound against each other; tensioning; testing by ear.
SL-SQ02-001.change: Raw-material scarcity, named in the sources as hides and wood, is an ongoing constraint that can be observed rather than asserted.
SL-SQ02-001.unresolved: Whether the hide shortage is a legal supply question, a wildlife-protection question or a price question. The sources name the shortage but not its cause.
SL-SQ02-001.access: No contact made. Schools and temples are named as customers, which gives a possible route through a dance school rather than through the workshop.
SL-SQ02-001.ethics: Animal hides are central to the craft. The subject must be handled factually, without either sensationalising it or concealing it, and the legal position on protected species must be checked before filming.

SL-SQ02-002.title: Cut with a thumbnail
SL-SQ02-002.premise: Laksha work applies resin from the lac insect to turned wood. In the niyapoten veda technique the lac is drawn out and severed with the thumbnail, and the finished piece is polished with a talipot leaf and coconut oil. Published accounts name Hapuwida in Matale as a village with a handful of remaining artisans, and at least one press piece is titled as being about Sri Lanka's last lacquer workers.
SL-SQ02-002.place: Hapuwida in Matale; Angulmaduwa near Tangalle; Hurikaduwa near Kandy; Pallekanda near Balangoda
SL-SQ02-002.activity: Breeding and collecting the lac resin, washing, drying and filtering it; heating; laying colour on a turning piece; severing with the thumbnail; polishing.
SL-SQ02-002.change: A named technique with a named village and a small, countable number of practitioners.
SL-SQ02-002.unresolved: How many artisans at Hapuwida still work niyapoten veda rather than brush or spray finishing. Not established.
SL-SQ02-002.ethics: The 'last practitioner' framing is used by several of these sources. It must be checked rather than adopted, because it is a framing that sells.

sources.supports: Press treatment of the remaining lacquer workers; to be read in full before any number is used.

sources.title: Traditional Laksha Industry in Sri Lanka - Ceylon Handicraft
sources.supports: The lac resin is secreted by an insect, bred on suitable trees, then scraped, washed, dried and filtered; the niyapoten veda technique uses the fingernail, and the piece is polished with a talipot leaf coated in coconut oil.

SL-SQ02-004.title: Two thousand hectares and one breath
SL-SQ02-004.premise: Na Uyana Aranya Senasanaya is a forest monastery spread over more than 2,000 hectares and described as home to roughly 150 monks, associated with the Sri Kalyani Yogasrama Samstha, with meditation practice following the Pa-Auk method. Cave dwellings with Brahmi inscriptions and stupa ruins at the site date to the third century BCE.
SL-SQ02-004.place: Na Uyana Aranya on the Dummiya range; comparable aranyas at Ritigala, Nissarana Vanaya and elsewhere
SL-SQ02-004.activity: Walking between kutis, alms round, the day's timetable, and long sitting. The observable material is the forest, the routine and the silence, not anyone's inner state.
SL-SQ02-004.change: Not established as an event. The monastery is a continuing institution, and a documentary would have to find its subject in a specific person's arrival, ordination or departure, which has not been identified.
SL-SQ02-004.unresolved: Whether any monastery would permit filming at all, and on what terms. Several aranyas do not admit visitors during the rains retreat.
SL-SQ02-004.access: No contact made. Permission runs through the monastery's chief incumbent and, for the Yogasrama group, through the parent body.

SL-SQ09-001.title: Not enough hands for the bark

SL-SQ11-003.place: Not established; sources cover southern Sri Lanka and national data

SL-SQ12-001.title: Paid to be photographed doing it

SL-SQ12-002.title: Giving the thing you need

SL-SQ12-002.place: Mobile camps at workplaces, schools and temples; the National Blood Centre in Colombo

SL-SQ20-001.place: Dry-zone cascades including the Palugaswewa cascade
SL-SQ20-001.activity: Desilting, bund repair, replanting the tank's forest belt, the seasonal filling and drawing down of a tank, and the farmer-organisation meetings where water is allocated.
SL-SQ20-001.change: Restoration work with dates, locations and participating communities, against a documented backdrop of neglect.
SL-SQ20-001.unresolved: Which specific cascade has work scheduled in the coming season, and whether a farmer organisation would welcome filming. Not established.
SL-SQ20-001.access: No contact made. Farmer organisations and the Department of Agrarian Development are the formal routes.
SL-SQ20-001.ethics: Water allocation is a source of dispute between upstream and downstream users. Filming one meeting can expose a position. Consent must cover the organisation, not only an individual speaker.

SL-SQ21-001.title: Five generations at the same mask bench
SL-SQ21-001.premise: Ambalangoda is the centre of Sri Lankan mask carving. Published accounts describe workshops held within one family across five generations, with carving, painting and a museum on the same premises.
SL-SQ21-001.activity: Drying and seasoning kaduru wood, roughing out the facial form with chisels, fine detail carving, paint preparation and painting; visitors passing through the museum while work continues behind it.
SL-SQ21-001.change: Not established. Whether the workshop is passing to a further generation, and on what terms, is exactly what research must find out rather than assume.
SL-SQ21-001.unresolved: Whether any workshop other than the well-known museum ones still carves for ritual use rather than for sale. The five-generation claim comes from the workshop's own presentation and needs an independent check.
SL-SQ21-001.access: No contact made. The museum workshops receive visitors, which makes an approach possible but also means the filmed version of the craft is already a performance for visitors. That has to be handled, not ignored.
SL-SQ21-001.ethics: Sanni masks belong to a healing ritual tradition. Filming the carving is not the same as filming a ritual, and the two must not be conflated for effect.

SL-SQ21-002.title: The model that has to be destroyed

SL-SQ21-002.change: Not established. Whether these workshops are producing for temples, for the domestic market or for tourist sale, and in what proportion, is a research question.
SL-SQ21-002.unresolved: Whether any workshop still casts by the full lost-wax method rather than reusing permanent moulds. This single question decides whether the premise holds, and it has not been answered.
SL-SQ21-002.access: No contact made. Pilimathalawa is a retail strip on a main road; the casting happens away from it.
SL-SQ21-002.ethics: Furnace work and molten metal. Safety and insurance for a crew, and for anyone asked to demonstrate a pour, must be settled first.

SL-SQ21-006.title: The building came back
SL-SQ21-006.premise: The library was burned on the night of 31 May 1981. At the time it held a reported 97,000 volumes, including ola-leaf manuscripts. It was partially reopened in 1984 and fully restored by 2003 through a programme with a reported restoration cost of around 700 million rupees, with international contributions and roughly 25,000 books collected; accounts record that it reopened largely without books.
SL-SQ21-006.activity: The reading rooms as they are used now, the catalogue, and whatever remains of the pre-1981 holdings.
SL-SQ21-006.change: Not a current event. The live question is what a restored institution can and cannot restore, and that is answerable by looking at the shelves.
SL-SQ21-006.unresolved: How many pre-1981 items survive, and whether any are catalogued as such. Attribution of responsibility for the burning is contested in the sources and must be reported as attributed, not asserted.
SL-SQ21-006.access: No contact made. The library is run by the Jaffna Municipal Council.
SL-SQ21-006.ethics: High. The event is part of a contested national history and any account of it will be read politically. The film should keep to what the library can show and to what the people who use it now say, rather than narrating the conflict over them.

SL-SQ22-001.title: Listening for the singing fish
SL-SQ22-001.premise: The Batticaloa lagoon is widely known as the place of the singing fish, a reported underwater sound heard on still nights. Scientific literature records that the lagoon, Sri Lanka's third-largest brackish water body, has undergone habitat degradation and water-quality deterioration over
SL-SQ22-001.place: Batticaloa lagoon, including the water near the Kallady bridge
SL-SQ22-001.activity: Night boats on the lagoon, listening with an oar or a hydrophone, the bridge, and the fishing that continues in the lagoon.
SL-SQ22-001.change: A remembered phenomenon against a documented decline in the water body itself.
SL-SQ22-001.unresolved: Whether the sound is currently audible, whether any recording of it exists that can be licensed, and which species is responsible. None of this is established, and the premise collapses into folklore if nothing can be heard. That is itself a legitimate outcome for a documentary, but it must be planned for.

SL-SQ22-003.unresolved: Whether any institution holds a catalogued Arwi collection, and whether anyone currently reads Arwi as a working skill. Both are unknown, and the second one decides whether there is a film here.
SL-SQ22-003.ethics: Kattankudy has a difficult recent history in national coverage. The film must not arrive there via that history, and the community's own priorities should shape whether this is worth doing at all.

SL-SQ23-001.unresolved: Every figure is from 2015 and must be re-counted for 2026. The allegation about political access to permits is an allegation reported by a newspaper; it is not established and must not be repeated as fact or put to anyone on camera as though it were.
SL-SQ23-001.access: No contact made. The craftsmen's association at Radawadunna is a plausible first approach and is a body rather than an individual.
SL-SQ23-001.ethics: The story touches on alleged corruption. Filming people who depend on permits, while that allegation is in the air, could expose them. Anonymity options must be settled before any approach.

SL-SQ23-002.title: Blaming the plastic pot
SL-SQ23-002.premise: Molagoda is described as one of the oldest continuously active clay-craft communities, with families whose pottery work descends from obligations under the rajakariya system. Published accounts attribute the industry's decline both to aluminium and plastic goods displacing clay cookware and to clay itself becoming scarce and expensive.
SL-SQ23-002.place: Molagoda near Kegalle on the Kandy-Colombo road; Dediyawala, Anguruwatota and Polgampola for clay
SL-SQ23-002.activity: Digging and preparing clay, wheel throwing, drying yards, open or kiln firing, roadside stalls.
SL-SQ23-002.change: At least two separate causes are documented for the same decline. The single-cause story that gets repeated is the plastic one.
SL-SQ23-002.unresolved: Who controls clay extraction licences, and whether construction demand is the competing use. Not established.
SL-SQ23-002.access: No contact made. Molagoda is a roadside pottery strip and is used to visitors, which again means the visible version may be the sales version.
SL-SQ23-002.ethics: Poverty is reported in the sources. It must not be filmed as picturesque, and no potter should be asked to perform hardship.

sources.title: Earthenware of Sri Lanka - Asia InCH
sources.supports: A clay variety from Dediyawela in Kalutara district mixed with welimetta; pottery villages in Kalutara include Dediyawala, Anguruwatota and Polgampola.

sources.title: Molagoda Pottery Village, Kegalle - Lakpura
sources.supports: Molagoda is about 12 km from Kegalle town on the Kandy-Colombo road; families have made clay pottery since the rajakariya period.

sources.title: Pottery of Sri Lanka - Wikipedia
sources.supports: Demand for traditional cookware declined with aluminium and plastic goods; clay has become a scarce resource, raising production costs.

SL-SQ23-003.title: The turbines and the fishing ground
SL-SQ23-003.premise: The Thambapavani wind farm on Mannar Island, operated by the Ceylon Electricity Board, was built along fishing routes in 2020. A second phase involving Adani Green Energy has been proposed with 52 turbines of 5.2 MW each in an area between a marine national park and a Ramsar wetland. Reporting records fishermen saying they were not told the project would change their livelihoods, concerns in an en
SL-SQ23-003.place: Mannar Island, between the Adam's Bridge Marine National Park and the Vankalai Ramsar wetland
SL-SQ23-003.activity: Launching and landing small craft, net work, the turbines themselves, protest meetings, and the bird migration that makes the site internationally significant.
SL-SQ23-003.change: An active, contested, currently unfolding project with documented objections and a documented legal and environmental dimension.
SL-SQ23-003.unresolved: Whether the second phase is proceeding as of 2026, and under which operator. Reporting is contested and politically charged, and allegations of cronyism appear in the press without being established.
SL-SQ23-003.access: No contact made. Fisher co-operative societies in Mannar are the appropriate first approach.
SL-SQ23-003.ethics: A live political dispute in a post-war district. Filming fishers who are in conflict with a state utility and a large investor can expose them. Allegations of cronyism reported in the press must not be repeated as fact or put to participants as though established.

SL-SQ23-004.title: Whose forest the field is
SL-SQ23-004.premise: Academic work on chena in Monaragala records the major problems reported by farmers as wildlife and cattle damage (83 per cent), legal action by the forest department (67 per cent), drought (65 per cent), pests and disease (54 per cent) and marketing (43 per cent), and records that around 74 per cent of respondents were willing to continue chena because they have no alternative livelihood. Satelli
SL-SQ23-004.place: Monaragala district, including the Maligavila area
SL-SQ23-004.activity: Clearing and burning before the north-east monsoon, sowing sesame, kurakkan, cowpea and maize, guarding against wildlife, and the harvest.
SL-SQ23-004.change: A seasonal cycle with a legal dispute running through it and a measured worsening of drought conditions.
SL-SQ23-004.unresolved: Whether any of the filmed cultivation would be legally exposed. This decides whether the story can be made at all without putting a household at risk of prosecution.
SL-SQ23-004.ethics: High and specific. Filming cultivation that a state department treats as illegal could produce evidence against the participants. This must be resolved with the participants and, if necessary, with the department before any filming, and anonymity may not be enough.

SL-SQ23-006.title: Seventeen hundred and fifty
SL-SQ23-006.premise: Reporting records an agreement signed in January 2026 raising the basic daily wage from 1,350 to 1,550 rupees with a further 200 rupees as a daily attendance allowance, giving 1,750 rupees in total, and records labour advocates warning that attendance-based incentives can still reduce what a worker actually earns. SL-SQ23-006.district: Nuwara Eliya, Badulla, Kandy, Ratnapura and others
SL-SQ23-006.activity: Plucking and weighing, the weighing shed, estate housing, union meetings, and the muster that the attendance allowance depends on.
SL-SQ23-006.change: A very recent, dated wage change whose real effect is disputed and is measurable at the weighing shed.
SL-SQ23-006.unresolved: What a worker actually received in a given month after the attendance condition. That is a payslip question and cannot be answered from reporting.
SL-SQ23-006.access: No contact made. Plantation companies control access to estates, which means the company is a gatekeeper to a story partly about the company.

Consent must include a clear account of that risk and a genuine option to withdraw or be unidentifiable. This community's history is also routinely told for it rather than by it, which the film should not repeat.

SL-SQ23-007.title: Who gets to name the reason the fare changed
SL-SQ23-007.premise: Reporting describes renewed protests by three-wheeler drivers in the last two weeks of December 2025 at Ella, Weligama and Sigiriya against app-based platforms, on the argument that their expansion is eroding livelihoods. SL-SQ23-007.activity: A three-wheeler stand, the protest itself, a driver's phone, and the negotiation at a tourist site.
SL-SQ23-007.change: A currently live dispute with dated protests and an unresolved regulatory question.
SL-SQ23-007.unresolved: Actual earnings before and after, on both sides of the argument. Neither drivers' nor platforms' figures have been independently checked.

SL-SQ23-008.title: The person who opens the sluice
SL-SQ23-008.premise: Sri Lanka is described as retaining around 10,000 village tanks of this type, many still irrigating paddy. Historically a vel vidane, a water master, administered the tank, received a share of each farmer's harvest and was responsible for coordinating maintenance and opening the sluice. Farmer Organisations in their current form came into operation in the 1980s, combining a committee with a water
SL-SQ23-008.place: Dry-zone villages with working small tanks
SL-SQ23-008.province: North Central, North Western, Uva, Eastern
SL-SQ23-008.activity: The kanna meeting where the season's water is agreed, the sluice being opened, the canal, and the fields that are at the end of it.
SL-SQ23-008.change: Seasonal and recurring: each cultivation season begins with a decision that has to be made and enforced by people who live together.
SL-SQ23-008.unresolved: Which village, and whether its next season's allocation meeting falls within a filming window. Not established.
SL-SQ23-008.access: No contact made. The Department of Agrarian Development registers farmer organisations and is the formal route.
SL-SQ23-008.ethics: Moderate to high. A water dispute filmed on one side can harden it. Consent should come from the organisation as well as from individuals, and the film must not adjudicate who is right.

SL-SQ23-009.title: The land under the settlement
SL-SQ23-009.premise: A survey is reported to have identified 68,812 families across 1,499 underserved settlements lacking adequate water, electricity and sanitation, with a programme planning 50,000 units to relocate them. Published research records that relocation began by demolishing settlements on the most valuable land, that families were offered a standard two-bedroom unit in any available complex regardless of t
SL-SQ23-009.place: Colombo's underserved settlements and the relocation housing complexes
SL-SQ23-009.activity: A flat in a tower, the block's shared spaces, the ground where a settlement stood, and a residents' meeting.
SL-SQ23-009.change: A programme that has moved a large number of people, with a live dispute about the conditions they were moved into.
SL-SQ23-009.unresolved: What happened to the vacated land in each case. That is checkable in land records and has not been checked.
SL-SQ23-009.access: No contact made. Residents' committees in the complexes are the appropriate route rather than the authority.

SL-SQ24-002.title: An argument conducted around an animal
SL-SQ24-002.premise: The Esala Perahera runs for ten nights ending on the Esala full moon; in 2025 it is reported as running from 30 July to 9 August. The Maligawa tusker carries the casket associated with the Tooth Relic. Reports describe elephant numbers rising to a hundred or more during the Randoli nights. The welfare argument around the use of captive elephants was NOT documented by the research done so far and r
SL-SQ24-002.activity: Preparation and caparisoning, the nightly processions, the mahouts' work, and whatever oversight or veterinary process exists.
SL-SQ24-002.change: A fixed annual event of very large scale. Whether anything is currently changing about how the elephants are used is not established.
SL-SQ24-002.unresolved: Everything about welfare, regulation, ownership and veterinary oversight. Without that, this is a spectacle, not a documentary, and it should not be scheduled on the strength of the procession alone.
SL-SQ24-002.access: No contact made. The Sri Dalada Maligawa administers the procession and controls access.
SL-SQ24-002.ethics: High and two-sided. The procession is a religious event of great importance to many people, and the captive-elephant question is genuinely contested. A film that arrives with a verdict on either side would be dishonest. Mahouts must not be made to answer for a national policy.

SL-SQ24-004.title: The price that is agreed at three in the morning
SL-SQ24-004.premise: The Dambulla centre, established in 1999 to decentralise produce marketing and give farmers better access, is described as the country's largest wholesale vegetable and fruit market, operating from early morning to midnight. Published accounts record farmers as about 36 per cent of weekly arrivals, with stall owners acting as intermediaries on commission, and describe the centre as having the lowe
SL-SQ24-004.activity: Lorries arriving through the night, unloading and weighing, the commission stalls, and the price being settled.
SL-SQ24-004.change: Nightly and dated. A farmer's whole season resolves into one number on one night.
SL-SQ24-004.unresolved: Who actually sets the opening price each night, and how. The mechanism is described differently by the operator and by the press.
SL-SQ24-004.access: No contact made. The centre is a public market, which makes observation straightforward.

SL-SQ24-005.title: A decision taken quickly and paid for slowly
SL-SQ24-005.premise: In April 2021 the government banned synthetic agrochemicals including chemical fertilisers, and lifted the ban in November 2021. A 2023 survey is reported as finding an average paddy yield loss of 53 per cent, with 62 per cent of farmers reporting more than 50 per cent loss, and a 32 per cent post-ban decline in rice yields against the previous nine years while the cultivated area was unchanged. P
SL-SQ24-005.activity: A field being prepared, the shop where fertiliser is bought, and the debt paperwork.
SL-SQ24-005.change: A completed policy reversal whose effects are still being carried, with measured figures on both sides.
SL-SQ24-005.unresolved: Whether any compensation scheme reached farmers, and what a household's debt actually looks like now. Not established.
SL-SQ24-005.access: No contact made. Farmer organisations are the route.
SL-SQ24-005.ethics: High. This is a politically charged failure and a film can easily become a partisan argument. Farmers' debts are private, and the organic-versus-chemical argument must not be settled on the back of one household's difficulty.
